articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment is part of OFAC's ongoing review and adjustment of sanctions guidance.
The specific details of the amendments were not immediately released, but such changes typically involve modifications to authorized transactions or activities under existing sanctions programs.
Entities engaging in Iran-related transactions are advised to review the updated General License to ensure continued compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities Tied to North Korea and DRC
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial activities and support networks.

The designations include 10 individuals and three entities added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list under North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo sanctions programs. Several entries carry restrictions under the North Korea Sanctions Regulations.

Among those designated are Russian and North Korean nationals linked to LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER. The Rwandan Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Kigali-based financial institution, were also added under DRC-related sanctions. These designations increase secondary sanctions risks for financial institutions and payment firms involved in transactions with these regions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to a $1,529,685 settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for nine apparent violations of Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services from the United States to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by the designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not on the SDN list at the time of the transactions.

OFAC determined the violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed. The Department of Justice also entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, imposing criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 for sanctions and export control offenses, with OFAC crediting the DOJ fine against its settlement.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Sanctions Law Center

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced amendments to 11 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, as part of its ongoing review of published guidance.

The revisions primarily address financial institutions' obligations when processing transactions involving sanctioned parties, maintaining blocked accounts, and submitting regulatory reports. Key updates include clarifying the distinction between blocking and rejecting transactions, guidance on interest requirements for blocked funds, and the deduction of service charges from blocked accounts.

The amended FAQs also distinguish preliminary customer inquiries from actual payment instructions, clarifying that merely asking about a prohibited transfer does not trigger blocking or rejection reporting obligations. Financial institutions are required to report blocked property and rejected transactions through OFAC's Reporting System within 10 business days.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / KPMG / Better Regulation

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New General Licenses, Amends FAQs, and Removes Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on October 21, 2026, including new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, amendments to Frequently Asked Questions, and the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations.

These actions reflect OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions implementation, balancing enforcement with humanitarian considerations and policy adjustments. The specific details of the new General Licenses and FAQ amendments were not immediately available.

The removal of designations for certain entities or individuals from Belarus and North Korea indicates a reassessment of their involvement in sanctioned activities or a change in their status. Affected parties should review the updated lists and guidance for compliance implications.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, along with the issuance of associated General Licenses.

These designations aim to combat intellectual property theft and protect American innovation by targeting individuals and entities involved in such illicit activities. The PAIPA provides new authorities for the U.S. government to impose sanctions in this critical area.

The accompanying General Licenses are intended to mitigate unintended consequences of the designations and ensure that certain legitimate transactions or activities can continue. Specific details of the designated parties and the scope of the General Licenses were not immediately provided.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026.

These updates are part of OFAC's ongoing adjustments to the Venezuela sanctions program, which often involve fine-tuning authorizations for certain transactions or activities to align with U.S. foreign policy objectives.
Parties involved in Venezuela-related dealings should review the amended General License and FAQ to understand any changes to permissible activities and ensure continued compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities, Issues New General Licenses for Iran and Cuba
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and Cuba designations on October 15, 2026, alongside the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.

These actions underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on Iran and Cuba through targeted sanctions. The designations aim to disrupt networks supporting activities deemed detrimental to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

The new and amended General Licenses and FAQs provide guidance on permissible transactions and activities, aiming to clarify the scope of the sanctions and minimize unintended impacts on legitimate trade and humanitarian efforts.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a change in the sanctioned status of a particular entity or individual.
Such removals typically occur when the designated party is deemed to no longer meet the criteria for designation, or when there are policy considerations that warrant delisting.

The removal of a designation can have significant implications for entities and individuals previously prohibited from engaging in transactions with the delisted party, opening avenues for renewed engagement.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing activities globally.
These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to disrupt and dismantle criminal and terrorist networks that pose a threat to international security and stability.

The designations impose severe restrictions on the designated parties, including blocking their assets and prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with them. This aims to isolate them from the international financial system.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Fined Over $1.5 Million by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and related services from the United States to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), which was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company.

OFAC determined that Extreme Networks acted with reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions by failing to conduct sufficient due diligence and heed warning signs that MMZA was the ultimate recipient of the goods. The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to an $11,662,930 settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred due to the bank processing payments involving blocked banks, failing to prioritize alerts for customers matching blocked persons, not promptly updating watchlists, and mishandling business accounts associated with blocked persons.

OFAC determined that Bank of America's apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. This settlement was part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury, which included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarding firm, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for four apparent violations of the Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and six apparent violations of the Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

Between September 2023 and February 2024, Pegasus dealt in blocked property by facilitating the importation of a machine supplied by a designated company, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., which was sanctioned for its involvement in the global illicit drug trade.
OFAC determined that Pegasus's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed. The company also failed to respond fully to an OFAC subpoena for six months, contributing to the penalty.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230 in Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle potential civil liability for apparent sanctions violations. The specific details of the violations were not immediately released but typically involve unauthorized transactions with sanctioned countries or individuals.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on individual accountability for sanctions breaches, alongside corporate entities.
Individuals engaged in international transactions are reminded of their obligations to comply with U.S. sanctions laws and to conduct thorough due diligence to avoid prohibited activities.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems Fined $60,764 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to a $60,764 settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for eight apparent violations of Iran sanctions.

The violations occurred when Rice Lake's Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) between July 2019 and November 2021, with knowledge that the goods were ultimately destined for Iran.

OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and non-egregious. The case underscores the importance of U.S. companies ensuring their foreign subsidiaries comply with U.S. sanctions, particularly in high-risk jurisdictions.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting Settles with OFAC for $1.05 Million Over Russia Sanctions Breach
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a Washington, D.C.-based global advisory firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions targeting Russia's financial sector.

Between April 2019 and May 2021, FTI indirectly dealt in the prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, a Russian state-owned bank on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification (SSI) List. FTI continued to provide services even as invoices went unpaid beyond the permissible 14-day tenor, effectively extending prohibited debt.

OFAC determined the apparent violations were non-egregious but not voluntarily self-disclosed. The penalty amount was aggravated to promote future compliance among similarly situated firms, with OFAC citing FTI's reckless disregard for warning signs.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275 Million by OFAC for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle 32 apparent violations of OFAC's Iran sanctions.

From November 2023 to June 2025, AEL caused U.S. financial institutions to process approximately $192 million in payments for 32 shipments of Iranian-origin liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) disguised as Omani and Iraqi product.

OFAC determined that AEL's apparent violations were egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, citing multiple red flags that the company either missed or dismissed without adequate investigation. This penalty represents a significant enforcement action against a foreign company for Iran-related sanctions evasion.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Akrivis Law Group, PLLC

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,110,661
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle potential civil liability for apparent sanctions violations. The specific details of the violations were not immediately released.
This settlement underscores OFAC's continued enforcement efforts across various financial sectors to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions programs.

Financial institutions and trading platforms are reminded of the critical importance of robust sanctions compliance programs, including customer screening and transaction monitoring, to prevent prohibited activities.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $3,777,000 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle potential civil liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations.

The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021, involving a U.S. citizen residing abroad. This case highlights OFAC's reach in enforcing sanctions against individuals, even those operating outside the United States.
The significant penalty emphasizes the serious consequences for individuals who engage in unauthorized transactions with sanctioned jurisdictions or entities.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Sanctions Law Center

articles.headline: IMG Academy Settles with OFAC for $1.72 Million Over Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle its potential civil liability for 89 apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions.

Between 2019 and 2025, IMG Academy dealt in the property or interests in property of two Specially Designated Nationals (SDNs) sanctioned for their ties to a Mexico-based drug cartel. The violations involved entering into tuition enrollment agreements and processing payments for the benefit of the designees' children.

OFAC found that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed that the individuals' names matched entries on the SDN List. The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the conduct was non-egregious but not voluntarily disclosed.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Sanctions Law Center

articles.headline: Global Markets React to Mixed Economic Signals Amid Inflation Concerns
body: Global financial markets are exhibiting mixed reactions as investors digest a series of economic signals, including persistent inflation concerns and varying central bank stances. Major indices have seen fluctuations throughout October, reflecting uncertainty about the pace of economic recovery and future monetary policy.

Energy prices, particularly for oil and natural gas, continue to be a significant factor influencing inflation. Supply chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions, and increased demand in certain sectors are contributing to upward price pressures, impacting consumer spending and corporate earnings.

Analysts are closely watching upcoming inflation reports and statements from key central banks, including the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, for indications of future interest rate adjustments. The interplay of these factors is expected to shape market sentiment in the coming months.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions Against Major Banks for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting significant penalties against major financial institutions for deficiencies in their Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance programs.

Bank of America, National Association, was assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for its deficient BSA/AML compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC noted that the bank's transaction monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, leading to numerous late Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs).

Additionally, American Express National Bank was issued a Cease and Desist Order and a civil money penalty for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, including failures in suspicious activity report filings and customer due diligence. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against individuals for embezzlement.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
